Recreating Figure 1, Class 2: Bar Plots and Gene Ontology (ER-mutant dataset)

2026-10-28

Getting Started

Code chunk options

Install the required R libraries

# CRAN
#install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2"))

# Bioconductor
#BiocManager::install(c("clusterProfiler", "org.Hs.eg.db", "enrichplot", "GO.db"), ask = FALSE)

Libraries loaded

# loading required packages
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(clusterProfiler)
library(enrichplot)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)   # human annotation database (Hs = Homo sapiens)

Packages only need to be installed once. After that, library() is enough.

Watch out: org.Hs.eg.db loads a function called select(), and so does dplyr. This is why we always write dplyr::select() and dplyr::filter(): the dplyr:: tells R exactly which package’s function to use.

Part 1: Finishing Figure 1C

Step 3e: A table of normalized counts with symbols

Step 1 Read in the normalized counts into an object called norm_counts.

norm_counts <- read.csv("ERmut_normalized_counts.csv", header = T)

head(norm_counts, 3)
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3 WT_veh_1
## 1 ENSG00000000003.15 ENSG00000000003 TSPAN6 2069.380 2028.608 1914.616 1910.285
## 2 ENSG00000000419.14 ENSG00000000419   DPM1 7143.445 6820.030 6337.237 5765.073
## 3 ENSG00000000457.14 ENSG00000000457  SCYL3 1631.421 1703.043 1527.447 1850.110
##   WT_veh_2 WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2  YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## 1 2132.058 2038.856 1655.170 1746.833 1773.702 1622.415 1825.956 1694.110
## 2 5795.568 6017.305 5987.946 6330.357 6265.083 6100.281 6394.979 6233.931
## 3 1842.981 1950.512 1494.002 1402.495 1455.297 1479.423 1557.433 1545.657
dim(norm_counts)
## [1] 23475    15

What is in each column?

Column What it is Example
ensembl_id_version The Ensembl ID with the version number (the row names from last class) ENSG00000000003.15
ensembl_id The Ensembl ID without the version number (Step 3c) ENSG00000000003
symbol The gene symbol we looked up with mapIds() (Step 3d) TSPAN6
WT_E2_1 … YS_veh_3 One column per sample: the normalized count 2069.38

  • Notice the counts are not whole numbers anymore. Each raw count was divided by that sample’s size factor, so samples sequenced to different depths can now be compared.

  • We have 23475 genes: the genes that were left after we removed genes with fewer than 10 reads (Step 1f).

Step 2 Read in the sample sheet. We will need it to know which sample belongs to which group.

sampleTable <- read.csv("sample_annotations.csv", header = T)

sampleTable
##      sample ER_status condition rep  group
## 1   WT_E2_1        WT        E2   1  WT_E2
## 2   WT_E2_2        WT        E2   2  WT_E2
## 3   WT_E2_3        WT        E2   3  WT_E2
## 4  WT_veh_1        WT       veh   1 WT_veh
## 5  WT_veh_2        WT       veh   2 WT_veh
## 6  WT_veh_3        WT       veh   3 WT_veh
## 7   YS_E2_1        YS        E2   1  YS_E2
## 8   YS_E2_2        YS        E2   2  YS_E2
## 9   YS_E2_3        YS        E2   3  YS_E2
## 10 YS_veh_1        YS       veh   1 YS_veh
## 11 YS_veh_2        YS       veh   2 YS_veh
## 12 YS_veh_3        YS       veh   3 YS_veh

✏️ Exercise 3.1 — Where is CASC5? Figure 1C shows two genes: CISH and CASC5. Use dplyr::filter() to find their rows. How many rows do you get?

norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% c("___", "___"))
Show solution 
norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% c("CISH", "CASC5"))
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3 WT_veh_1
## 1 ENSG00000114737.16 ENSG00000114737   CISH 1330.375 1504.336 1612.361 503.8245
##   WT_veh_2 WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2 YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2 YS_veh_3
## 1 473.3749 525.0997 1657.728 1480.108 1699.72 1571.818 1459.939 1691.927

Only one row: CISH. CASC5 is missing because the gene has been renamed.

%in% asks, for every row, “is this symbol one of the ones in my list?” and filter() keeps the rows where the answer is TRUE.

So what is CASC5 called now? The org.Hs.eg.db dictionary also stores old names as ALIAS. We can use mapIds() to go from alias to official symbol:

mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db,
       keys = "CASC5",       # the name we have
       keytype = "ALIAS",    # what kind of name it is (an old name)
       column = "SYMBOL")    # what we want back (the official name)
##  CASC5 
## "KNL1"

CASC5’s official symbol is now KNL1 (kinetochore scaffold 1). We’ll use the current name, and remember that it is called CASC5 in the paper.

Step 3 Save the two gene names in a vector, so we don’t have to type them again.

genes_fig1c <- c("CISH", "KNL1")

norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% genes_fig1c)
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol  WT_E2_1  WT_E2_2  WT_E2_3

## 2 ENSG00000137812.20 ENSG00000137812   KNL1 2095.773 1515.562 1788.255
##    WT_veh_1  WT_veh_2  WT_veh_3  YS_E2_1  YS_E2_2  YS_E2_3 YS_veh_1 YS_veh_2
## 1  503.8245  473.3749  525.0997 1657.728 1480.108 1699.720 1571.818 1459.939
## 2 1818.2518 1859.8208 1763.8981 3595.155 3864.240 3925.744 3650.709 3744.450

Step 4: The bar plots, Figure 1C

Open the paper and look at Figure 1C:

  • What is on the y-axis? What does “relative to WT DMSO” mean?
  • What do the error bars and stars mean? (Read the figure legend.)

4a. From wide to long format

norm_counts is in wide format: one row per gene, one column per sample. ggplot2 likes long format: one row per gene per sample.

Wide (one row per gene) Long (one row per gene per sample)
symbol WT_E2_1 WT_E2_2 ... → symbol sample norm_count
CISH 1520 1490 ... CISH WT_E2_1 1520
CISH WT_E2_2 1490 
fig1c_long <- norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% genes_fig1c) |>                # 1. keep only CISH and KNL1
  dplyr::select(-ensembl_id_version, -ensembl_id) |>       # 2. drop the two ID columns
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -symbol,                      # 3. turn every column except symbol...
                      names_to = "sample",                 #    ...column names go into "sample"
                      values_to = "norm_count") |>         #    ...the numbers go into "norm_count"
  dplyr::left_join(sampleTable, by = "sample")             # 4. add the sample sheet information

fig1c_long
## # A tibble: 24 × 7
##    symbol sample   norm_count ER_status condition   rep group 
##    <chr>  <chr>         <dbl> <chr>     <chr>     <int> <chr> 
##  1 CISH   WT_E2_1       1330. WT        E2            1 WT_E2 
##  2 CISH   WT_E2_2       1504. WT        E2            2 WT_E2 
##  3 CISH   WT_E2_3       1612. WT        E2            3 WT_E2 
##  4 CISH   WT_veh_1       504. WT        veh           1 WT_veh
##  5 CISH   WT_veh_2       473. WT        veh           2 WT_veh
##  6 CISH   WT_veh_3       525. WT        veh           3 WT_veh
##  7 CISH   YS_E2_1       1658. YS        E2            1 YS_E2 
##  8 CISH   YS_E2_2       1480. YS        E2            2 YS_E2 
##  9 CISH   YS_E2_3       1700. YS        E2            3 YS_E2 
## 10 CISH   YS_veh_1      1572. YS        veh           1 YS_veh
## # ℹ 14 more rows

What is each line doing?

  1. filter() keeps the 2 rows we want.
  2. select(-...): the minus sign means “remove this column”. We only want symbol and the 12 sample columns.
  3. pivot_longer(cols = -symbol) stacks the 12 sample columns into two new columns: sample (the old column name) and norm_count (the number). 2 genes × 12 samples = 24 rows.
  4. left_join() matches the sample column in our table with the sample column in sampleTable, and adds ER_status, condition, rep and group to every row.

4b. Relative expression

Figure 1C shows expression relative to WT DMSO: for each gene, the average of the 3 WT DMSO samples is set to 1, and every sample is divided by that average. A value of 2 means “twice as much as WT DMSO”.

\[\text{relative expression} = \frac{\text{normalized count of this sample}}{\text{average normalized count of the WT DMSO samples}}\]

✏️ Exercise 4.1 — Pick the reference group. Fill in the blank with the group that everything should be relative to.

fig1c_long <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_expr = norm_count / mean(norm_count[group == "___"])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
Show solution 
fig1c_long <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_expr = norm_count / mean(norm_count[group == "WT_veh"])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

What is it doing?

  • group_by(symbol) makes sure each gene is divided by its own WT DMSO average (CISH by CISH’s, KNL1 by KNL1’s).
  • norm_count[group == "WT_veh"] picks out only the 3 WT DMSO values; mean() averages them.
  • mutate() adds the result as a new column called rel_expr.
  • ungroup() removes the grouping, so it doesn’t affect later steps.

Check: the three WT_veh samples should now average to exactly 1 for each gene.

fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::filter(group == "WT_veh") |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr))
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   symbol mean_rel
##   <chr>     <dbl>
## 1 CISH          1
## 2 KNL1          1

4c. Mean ± SEM

Each bar is the mean of 3 replicates, and the error bar is the standard error of the mean (SEM):

\[\text{SEM} = \frac{\text{standard deviation}}{\sqrt{n}}\]

fig1c_summary <- fig1c_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol, group, ER_status, condition) |>   # one row per gene per group
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr),                # bar height
                   sem_rel = sd(rel_expr) / sqrt(n()),       # error bar
                   .groups = "drop")

fig1c_summary
## # A tibble: 8 × 6
##   symbol group  ER_status condition mean_rel sem_rel
##   <chr>  <chr>  <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 CISH   WT_E2  WT        E2           2.96   0.164 
## 2 CISH   WT_veh WT        veh          1      0.0300
## 3 CISH   YS_E2  YS        E2           3.22   0.134 
## 4 CISH   YS_veh YS        veh          3.14   0.134 
## 5 KNL1   WT_E2  WT        E2           0.992  0.0924
## 6 KNL1   WT_veh WT        veh          1      0.0153
## 7 KNL1   YS_E2  YS        E2           2.09   0.0560
## 8 KNL1   YS_veh YS        veh          2.05   0.0191
  • summarise() reduces the 3 replicates of each group to one row. 24 rows become 2 genes × 4 groups = 8 rows.
  • n() counts the rows in each group (here 3).
  • We include ER_status and condition in group_by() only so they stay in the table. We need ER_status to color the bars.

Assign factor levels. The paper orders bars WT DMSO, WT E2, Y537S DMSO, Y537S E2. Otherwise R uses alphabetical order.

group_order <- c("WT_veh", "WT_E2", "YS_veh", "YS_E2")

fig1c_long$group <- factor(fig1c_long$group, levels = group_order)
fig1c_summary$group <- factor(fig1c_summary$group, levels = group_order)

4d. Our first bar plot

✏️ Exercise 4.2 — Which columns go where? Each bar is a group, the height is the mean relative expression, and the bar color shows the genotype. Fill in the blanks.

ggplot(fig1c_summary, aes(x = ___, y = ___, fill = ___)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y")
Show solution 
ggplot(fig1c_summary, aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y")

  • geom_col() draws bars whose height is the y value.
  • facet_wrap(~ symbol) makes one small panel per gene.
  • scales = "free_y" lets each gene have its own y-axis range.

4e. Polish the figure

This plot uses two data frames: the bars and error bars come from fig1c_summary (one row per group), and the dots come from fig1c_long (one row per sample). That’s why we leave ggplot() empty and give each layer its own data =.

fig1c_plot <- ggplot() +
  # bars: the mean of each group
  geom_col(data = fig1c_summary,
           aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status),
           color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  # error bars: mean - SEM to mean + SEM
  geom_errorbar(data = fig1c_summary,
                aes(x = group, ymin = mean_rel - sem_rel, ymax = mean_rel + sem_rel),
                width = 0.25) +
  # dots: the individual replicates
  geom_point(data = fig1c_long,
             aes(x = group, y = rel_expr),
             size = 1.5,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = 1)) +
  # dashed line at 1 = same as WT DMSO
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "ESR1 status",
                    values = c(WT = "steelblue", YS = "darkorange"),
                    labels = c(WT = "WT", YS = "Y537S")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(WT_veh = "DMSO", WT_E2 = "E2",
                              YS_veh = "DMSO", YS_E2 = "E2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Relative expression\n(relative to WT DMSO)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3), face = "italic"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.1), colour = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom")

fig1c_plot

Code What it does
position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = 1) Spreads the dots a little left/right so they don’t sit on top of each other. seed = 1 makes the spread the same every time you run it
scale_fill_manual() WT in blue, Y537S in orange, and nicer legend labels
scale_x_discrete(labels = ...) Shows “DMSO”/“E2” under the bars instead of WT_veh, WT_E2, …
expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)) Bars start right at 0, with 15% empty space on top (room for the stars)
face = "italic" Gene names are written in italics

Question: Look at CISH. In WT cells, what does E2 do? In Y537S cells, is CISH already high without E2? This is what the authors call ligand-independent. Now look at KNL1: does E2 change it in WT cells? Why do the authors call it mutant-specific?

4f. Significance stars

The figure legend says: “Student two-sample t test was used: **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001; n.s., not significant.” Each bar is compared with WT DMSO.

✏️ Exercise 4.3 — One t-test by hand. Compare CISH in WT_E2 vs WT_veh. Fill in the two group names.

cish <- fig1c_long |> dplyr::filter(symbol == "CISH")

t.test(cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "___"],
       cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "___"],
       var.equal = TRUE)
Show solution 
cish <- fig1c_long |> dplyr::filter(symbol == "CISH")

t.test(cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_E2"],
       cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_veh"],
       var.equal = TRUE)
## 
##  Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_E2"] and cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_veh"]
## t = 11.755, df = 4, p-value = 0.0002996
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  1.497215 2.423140
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y 
##  2.960178  1.000000
  • cish$rel_expr[cish$group == "WT_E2"] = the 3 relative expression values of the WT E2 samples.
  • var.equal = TRUE makes it a classic Student’s t-test, as in the paper.
  • The number we need is the p-value.

Doing this by hand for 2 genes × 3 groups would be 6 t-tests. Instead, we let R do one t-test per row of the summary table.

fig1c_stats <- fig1c_summary |>
  dplyr::filter(group != "WT_veh") |>          # 1. we don't compare WT DMSO with itself
  dplyr::rowwise() |>                          # 2. do the next step one row at a time
  dplyr::mutate(
    # 3. t-test: this row's gene and group vs. the same gene in WT DMSO
    p_value = t.test(
      fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == group],
      fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == "WT_veh"],
      var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,
    # 4. the tallest replicate in this group, so the star sits above every point
    ymax = max(fig1c_long$rel_expr[fig1c_long$symbol == symbol & fig1c_long$group == group])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  # 5. turn the p-value into stars, using the cutoffs from the figure legend
  dplyr::mutate(label = dplyr::case_when(p_value < 0.0001 ~ "****",
                                         p_value < 0.001  ~ "***",
                                         p_value < 0.01   ~ "**",
                                         TRUE             ~ "n.s."))

fig1c_stats |> dplyr::select(symbol, group, mean_rel, p_value, label)
## # A tibble: 6 × 5
##   symbol group  mean_rel    p_value label
##   <chr>  <fct>     <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>
## 1 CISH   WT_E2     2.96  0.000300   ***  
## 2 CISH   YS_E2     3.22  0.0000866  **** 
## 3 CISH   YS_veh    3.14  0.0000975  **** 
## 4 KNL1   WT_E2     0.992 0.938      n.s. 
## 5 KNL1   YS_E2     2.09  0.0000469  **** 
## 6 KNL1   YS_veh    2.05  0.00000177 ****

What is it doing?

  1. filter(group != "WT_veh"): != means “is not equal to”. We are left with 6 rows (2 genes × 3 groups).
  2. rowwise(): normally mutate() works on a whole column at once. rowwise() tells it to work one row at a time, so inside mutate(), symbol and group mean “the value in this row”.
  3. The t.test() is exactly the one from Exercise 4.3, but instead of typing "CISH" and "WT_E2" we use symbol and group from the current row. $p.value pulls out just the p-value.
  4. max() finds the highest dot in that group. We’ll put the star a little above it.
  5. case_when() goes through the conditions in order and uses the first one that is TRUE. TRUE ~ "n.s." at the end means “everything else”.

Add the stars just above the tallest point in each group:

fig1c_final <- fig1c_plot +
  geom_text(data = fig1c_stats,
            aes(x = group, y = ymax * 1.08, label = label),
            size = 4.5)

fig1c_final

y = ymax * 1.08 places each label 8% above the tallest dot.

Save the figure.

ggsave("Fig1C_barplots_CISH_KNL1.png", fig1c_final, width = 7, height = 4.5)

“Black Trail” Exercise 1: GREB1

Scenario: Alex, a rotation student in the Gertz lab, measures GREB1 by qPCR every week as a quick read-out of “is ER active?”. GREB1 is one of the best-known estrogen-responsive genes in breast cancer, but it isn’t in Figure 1C.

Alex’s hypothesis: GREB1 is turned on by E2 in WT cells, and is already “on” in Y537S cells even without E2 (like CISH).

Help Alex make a Figure 1C-style bar plot for GREB1.

Hint: Everything you need is in Step 4. Use new object names starting with greb1_ so you don’t overwrite the CISH/KNL1 objects. Since there is only one gene, you don’t need group_by(symbol).

Show solution 
greb1_long <- norm_counts |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol == "GREB1") |>
  dplyr::select(-ensembl_id_version, -ensembl_id) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -symbol,
                      names_to = "sample",
                      values_to = "norm_count") |>
  dplyr::left_join(sampleTable, by = "sample") |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_expr = norm_count / mean(norm_count[group == "WT_veh"]))
greb1_summary <- greb1_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(symbol, group, ER_status, condition) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_expr),
                   sem_rel = sd(rel_expr) / sqrt(n()),
                   .groups = "drop")

greb1_long$group <- factor(greb1_long$group, levels = group_order)
greb1_summary$group <- factor(greb1_summary$group, levels = group_order)

Copy the code from Step 4e and change the three data = arguments:

greb1_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = greb1_summary,
           aes(x = group, y = mean_rel, fill = ER_status),
           color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(data = greb1_summary,
                aes(x = group, ymin = mean_rel - sem_rel, ymax = mean_rel + sem_rel),
                width = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = greb1_long,
             aes(x = group, y = rel_expr),
             size = 1.5,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, seed = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ symbol, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "ESR1 status",
                    values = c(WT = "steelblue", YS = "darkorange"),
                    labels = c(WT = "WT", YS = "Y537S")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(WT_veh = "DMSO", WT_E2 = "E2",
                              YS_veh = "DMSO", YS_E2 = "E2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Relative expression\n(relative to WT DMSO)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3), face = "italic"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.1), colour = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom")

greb1_plot

#ggsave("GREB1_barplot_WT_vs_Y537S.png", greb1_plot, width = 4, height = 4.5)

Was Alex right? Partly. GREB1 goes up strongly with E2 in WT cells (about 3.4×). In Y537S DMSO it is higher than in WT DMSO (about 1.7×), so the mutant ER does turn it on without estrogen, but not nearly as much as estrogen does in WT cells. Adding E2 to Y537S cells only raises it a little more.

Part 2: Gene Ontology, Figure 1D

Our next goal

Look at Figure 1D (the orange table is for Y537S). Read the figure legend and answer:

  • Which genes were used for this table?
  • What does the Direction column mean?
  • What kinds of biological processes go up in Y537S cells? Which go down?

The goal of functional analysis is to provide biological insight, so it’s important to interpret our results in the context of the question: Does mutant ER just act like WT ER that is always stimulated by estrogen, or does it also change new genes? If it changes new genes, what do those genes do?

GO Ontologies

The Gene Ontology (GO) knowledgebase is the world’s largest source of information on the function of genes. GO terms are organized into three independent controlled vocabularies (ontologies) in a species-independent manner:

  • Biological process (BP): the biological role of the gene, e.g. “cell division”, “DNA repair”, “apoptosis”.

  • Molecular function (MF): the biochemical activity of the gene product, e.g. “chromatin binding”, “GTPase activity”.

  • Cellular component (CC): where in the cell the gene product is found, e.g. “nucleus”, “vacuole”, “plasma membrane”.

Each GO term has a term name (e.g. DNA repair) and a unique term accession number (GO:0006281), and a single gene can be associated with many GO terms.

Question: Look at Figure 1D again. “Vacuole” and “Chromatin binding” are not biological processes. Which ontologies do they come from?

clusterProfiler

We will be using clusterProfiler to perform over-representation analysis on GO terms associated with our list of significant genes.

Over-representation analysis (ORA) asks: Are genes from a GO term present in my gene list more often than expected by chance?

Example: Imagine a bag of 10,000 marbles (all the genes we measured). 200 of them are red (genes in the “cell division” GO term), so 2% of the bag is red. You grab 500 marbles (your significant genes).

  • By chance, you’d expect about 2% of them to be red: 500 × 0.02 = 10 red marbles.
  • If you got 50 red marbles, that’s 5 times more than expected. Something about how you picked them isn’t random: “cell division” is over-represented in your list.

clusterProfiler does this for every GO term, and uses a hypergeometric test (the statistics of drawing marbles from a bag) to give each term a p-value. It needs two inputs:

List Also called The marbles…
Significant genes genes of interest …you grabbed
Background genes universe …in the whole bag

Where did the DESeq2 results come from?

For GO we need a list of genes that changed between two groups. That list comes from the DESeq2 results. We won’t rerun DESeq2 today. The two results files are already in the folder. This section explains how they were made, so you know what is inside them.

Which comparisons can we make?

Last class we built the DESeqDataSet with design = ~ group. The group column has 4 groups, and DESeq2 can compare any two of them. With 4 groups there are 6 pairwise comparisons:

# Comparison (numerator vs denominator) The question it answers Saved as a file?
1 WT_E2 vs WT_veh Which genes respond to estrogen in normal (WT) cells? yes
2 YS_veh vs WT_veh Which genes are different in mutant cells, without estrogen? yes
3 YS_E2 vs YS_veh Which genes respond to estrogen in mutant cells? no
4 YS_E2 vs WT_E2 Which genes are different in mutant cells when both get estrogen? no
5 YS_veh vs WT_E2 Does mutant ER without estrogen look like WT ER with estrogen? no
6 YS_E2 vs WT_veh Mutant + estrogen vs the untreated normal cells (two changes at once) no

We only saved #1 and #2, because those are the two questions Figure 1 asks:

  • #2 gives us the genes that change in Y537S cells (today’s GO input).
  • #1 tells us which of those genes are ordinary estrogen genes, so we can remove them in Step 6.

Question: Comparison #6 changes two things at once (genotype and treatment). If a gene is different in #6, can you tell which change caused it?

Which R object made them?

All 6 comparisons come from the same object: dds, the DESeqDataSet we built in Step 1e and ran DESeq() on in Step 1g. DESeq() already did the statistics for every group. The function results() just pulls out one comparison.

# BASIC USAGE
## DO NOT RUN
#res <- results(dds,
               #contrast = c("column in the sample sheet", "numerator group", "denominator group"))
Part of contrast Our value Meaning
1st "group" The column of the sample sheet that holds the groups (the one in design = ~ group)
2nd "YS_veh" The numerator: the top of the fold change
3rd "WT_veh" The denominator: the bottom of the fold change, our reference

The order matters. log2FoldChange = log2(numerator ÷ denominator). A positive value means the gene is higher in the numerator (here, higher in Y537S). If you swapped the two groups, every log2FoldChange would flip sign.

This is the code that was run last class (Step 5) to make the Y537S file. Don’t run it today: dds isn’t in your environment.

# 1. pull out one comparison from dds: Y537S DMSO vs WT DMSO
res_YS <- results(dds, contrast = c("group", "YS_veh", "WT_veh"))

# 2. turn it into a normal data frame, and move the gene IDs out of the row names into a column
res_YS_df <- as.data.frame(res_YS) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("ensembl_id_version")

# 3. add the Ensembl ID without version and the gene symbol (from Steps 3c and 3d last class)
res_YS_df$ensembl_id <- ensembl_ids
res_YS_df$symbol <- symbols

# 4. save it as a CSV file
write.csv(res_YS_df, "ERmut_DESeq2_YS_veh_vs_WT_veh.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The E2 file was made the same way, using contrast = c("group", "WT_E2", "WT_veh"). (In the CSV files, ensembl_id and symbol sit right after ensembl_id_version.)

Comparison R code Output file
#1 E2 in WT cells results(dds, contrast = c("group", "WT_E2", "WT_veh")) ERmut_DESeq2_WT_E2_vs_WT_veh.csv
#2 Y537S vs WT, no E2 results(dds, contrast = c("group", "YS_veh", "WT_veh")) ERmut_DESeq2_YS_veh_vs_WT_veh.csv

The file name tells you the comparison: numerator_vs_denominator.

✏️ Exercise 5.0 — Write the contrast. Which contrast would answer comparison #3: Which genes respond to estrogen in mutant cells? (Just write it down; we can’t run it today.)

Show solution

results(dds, contrast = c("group", "YS_E2", "YS_veh")). The numerator is the treated group, the denominator is the untreated group of the same genotype.

Step 5: Prepping the data

Step 1 Read in the Y537S vs WT results table.

res_YS <- read.csv("ERmut_DESeq2_YS_veh_vs_WT_veh.csv", header = T)

## 6 ENSG00000000971.16 ENSG00000000971    CFH    3.461826    -1.54461772
##        lfcSE      stat       pvalue         padj
## 1 0.06705896 -3.599229 3.191619e-04 8.553151e-04

## 3 0.06436658 -4.661790 3.134713e-06 1.032713e-05
## 4 0.08464321 10.033597 1.084903e-23 9.221881e-23
## 5 1.40287707  3.490618 4.819048e-04 1.262523e-03
## 6 1.23731542 -1.248362 2.118985e-01 3.143244e-01
dim(res_YS)
## [1] 23475     9

One row = one gene. These are the 23475 genes that passed our “at least 10 reads” filter last class. What is in each column? Here is the row for CISH:

res_YS |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol == "CISH")
##   ensembl_id_version      ensembl_id symbol baseMean log2FoldChange      lfcSE
## 1 ENSG00000114737.16 ENSG00000114737   CISH 1292.551       1.652253 0.09228909
##       stat       pvalue         padj
## 1 17.90301 1.117158e-71 3.449616e-70
Column Where it came from What it means CISH
ensembl_id_version Row names of dds Ensembl ID with version number ENSG00000114737.16
ensembl_id Step 3c last class Ensembl ID without version number ENSG00000114737
symbol Step 3d last class (mapIds()) Gene symbol CISH
baseMean DESeq2 The average normalized count across all 12 samples. How highly expressed the gene is overall ~1293
log2FoldChange DESeq2 log2(Y537S DMSO ÷ WT DMSO). How much the gene changed 1.65 (21.65 ≈ 3.1× higher in Y537S)
lfcSE DESeq2 The standard error of the log2 fold change: how uncertain that estimate is. Small = the replicates agree 0.09
stat DESeq2 The test statistic: log2FoldChange ÷ lfcSE. Big (+ or −) = a big change compared to the noise 17.9
pvalue DESeq2 The p-value from that test 1.1e-71
padj DESeq2 The p-value adjusted for testing ~23,000 genes at once. This is the one we use 3.4e-70

Why are some padj values NA? 1366 genes have a pvalue but no padj. DESeq2 does independent filtering: before adjusting, it drops genes whose counts are too low to ever be significant, so the multiple-testing penalty is smaller for the rest. Those genes get padj = NA. subset(padj < 0.05) will drop them when we make the significant list.

Question: Find KNL1 in res_YS. Is it higher or lower in Y537S cells? About how many times?

Step 2 Select the columns we need.

YS_background <- dplyr::select(res_YS,
                               ensembl_id,
                               symbol,
                               log2FoldChange,
                               padj)

head(YS_background)
##        ensembl_id symbol log2FoldChange         padj
## 1 ENSG00000000003 TSPAN6    -0.24136057 8.553151e-04
## 2 ENSG00000000419   DPM1     0.09171875 1.015181e-01
## 3 ENSG00000000457  SCYL3    -0.30006344 1.032713e-05
## 4 ENSG00000000460  FIRRM     0.84927592 9.221881e-23
## 5 ENSG00000000938    FGR     4.89690790 1.262523e-03
## 6 ENSG00000000971    CFH    -1.54461772 3.143244e-01
Column Meaning
ensembl_id Gene ID (no version number). This is the ID we give to clusterProfiler
symbol Gene symbol, for us humans
log2FoldChange How much the gene changed: log2(Y537S ÷ WT)
padj Adjusted p-value: how confident we are that the change is real

Background gene set

The background is every gene that could have ended up in our significant list: all 23475 genes DESeq2 tested. These are genes that are expressed in T-47D cells (they passed our “at least 10 reads” filter in Step 1f).

# we want the log2 fold change
original_gene_list <- YS_background$log2FoldChange

head(original_gene_list)
## [1] -0.24136057  0.09171875 -0.30006344  0.84927592  4.89690790 -1.54461772

Right now this is just a list of numbers. We don’t know which gene each number belongs to! So we name each number with its Ensembl ID:

# name the vector
names(original_gene_list) <- YS_background$ensembl_id

head(original_gene_list)
## ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000419 ENSG00000000457 ENSG00000000460 ENSG00000000938 
##     -0.24136057      0.09171875     -0.30006344      0.84927592      4.89690790 
## ENSG00000000971 
##     -1.54461772
# omit any NA values
background_gene_list <- na.omit(original_gene_list)
# sort the list in decreasing order (required for clusterProfiler)
background_gene_list <- sort(background_gene_list, decreasing = TRUE)
head(background_gene_list)
## ENSG00000174611 ENSG00000136542 ENSG00000230314 ENSG00000278621 ENSG00000152661 
##       10.207741       10.140600        8.780805        8.634743        8.605097 
## ENSG00000179388 
##        8.442037
length(background_gene_list)
## [1] 23475

Question: Why not use all ~60,000 human genes as the background? Many of them (e.g. hemoglobin, insulin, neuron genes) are not expressed in breast cancer cells, so they could never show up in our list. Adding them would make the bag bigger, so our list would look “special” for terms that are simply expressed in breast cancer cells. The p-values would look better than they really are.

Setting the cutoffs

Now we need to decide which genes are significant. We’ll use two cutoffs, and a gene has to pass both:

Cutoff Code What it asks
Adjusted p-value < 0.05 padj < 0.05 Are we confident the change is real (not just noise between replicates)?
Absolute log2 fold change > 1 abs(log2FoldChange) > 1 Is the change big enough to matter (at least 2-fold, up or down)?

What does a log2 fold change mean?

log2FoldChange Fold change (Y537S ÷ WT) In words
2 22 = 4 4 times higher in Y537S
1 21 = 2 2 times higher
0 20 = 1 no change
−1 2−1 = 0.5 2 times lower (half)
−2 2−2 = 0.25 4 times lower

So log2FoldChange > 1 means “at least 2-fold up”, and log2FoldChange < -1 means “at least 2-fold down”. abs() (absolute value) removes the minus sign, so abs(log2FoldChange) > 1 catches both directions at once.

Why do we need both cutoffs? Let’s count how many genes pass each one.

# how many genes have padj < 0.05?
sum(YS_background$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] 11195

11195 genes, about half of all the genes we tested! With 3 replicates and deep sequencing, DESeq2 can be confident about very small changes (e.g. 10%). Those genes are “real” but probably not very important biologically, and a list of 11,000 genes is too long to tell us anything.

# how many genes have padj < 0.05 AND at least a 2-fold change?
sum(YS_background$padj < 0.05 & abs(YS_background$log2FoldChange) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] 3453

Adding the fold-change cutoff leaves 3453 genes that changed reliably and strongly.

  • & means AND: both conditions must be TRUE.
  • sum() of TRUE/FALSE values counts the TRUEs (R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0).
  • na.rm = TRUE skips genes where padj is NA. DESeq2 sets padj to NA for genes with very low counts or an outlier sample.

Note: 0.05 and 2-fold are common choices, not laws of nature. Always report the cutoffs you used in your methods.

Significant gene set

Now we apply the cutoffs, one step at a time.

Cutoff 1: padj < 0.05

# Extract significant results (padj < 0.05) using subset()
sig_genes_df <- subset(YS_background, padj < 0.05)

nrow(sig_genes_df)
## [1] 11195

subset() keeps the rows where the condition is TRUE. It also drops rows where padj is NA, which is what we want.

Cutoff 2: |log2FC| > 1

# From significant results, we want the log2 fold change
sig_genes <- sig_genes_df$log2FoldChange

# Name the vector with the Ensembl IDs
names(sig_genes) <- sig_genes_df$ensembl_id

# omit NA values
sig_genes <- na.omit(sig_genes)

head(sig_genes)
## ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000457 ENSG00000000460 ENSG00000000938 ENSG00000001036 
##      -0.2413606      -0.3000634       0.8492759       4.8969079       0.3316309 
## ENSG00000001084 
##       0.1992452
# filter on min log2fold change (|log2FoldChange| > 1)
sig_genes <- names(sig_genes)[abs(sig_genes) > 1]

head(sig_genes)
## [1] "ENSG00000000938" "ENSG00000001461" "ENSG00000003137" "ENSG00000004478"
## [5] "ENSG00000004948" "ENSG00000005001"
length(sig_genes)
## [1] 3453

That last line packs in a lot. Reading it from the inside out:

  1. abs(sig_genes) removes the minus signs (−1.8 becomes 1.8), so up and down genes are treated the same.
  2. > 1 gives one TRUE/FALSE per gene: is the change bigger than 2-fold?
  3. names(sig_genes) gives the Ensembl IDs we attached in the previous chunk.
  4. [ ] with TRUE/FALSE inside keeps only the IDs where the answer was TRUE.

The result is a plain list of gene IDs (no numbers anymore). That’s exactly what enrichGO() wants.

✏️ Exercise 5.1 — Change the cutoff. How many genes pass if we use a 1.5-fold cutoff instead of 2-fold? (Hint: log2(1.5) ≈ 0.58.) And a 4-fold cutoff?

sum(abs(sig_genes_df$log2FoldChange) > ___)
Show solution 
sum(abs(sig_genes_df$log2FoldChange) > 0.58)   # 1.5-fold
## [1] 5930
sum(abs(sig_genes_df$log2FoldChange) > 2)      # 4-fold
## [1] 1371

A stricter cutoff gives a shorter list. Too short, and there aren’t enough genes to find enriched terms; too long, and the list is full of small changes.

Splitting into Up and Down

Figure 1D has a Direction column, so we need up and down genes as separate lists. This time we don’t use abs(), because the sign matters:

# keep the log2FC values of the significant genes (padj < 0.05)
YS_lfc <- sig_genes_df$log2FoldChange
names(YS_lfc) <- sig_genes_df$ensembl_id

# Up in Y537S: at least 2-fold higher
up_genes <- names(YS_lfc)[YS_lfc > 1]

# Down in Y537S: at least 2-fold lower
down_genes <- names(YS_lfc)[YS_lfc < -1]

length(up_genes)
## [1] 1629
length(down_genes)
## [1] 1824

Check: length(up_genes) + length(down_genes) should equal length(sig_genes).

length(up_genes) + length(down_genes) == length(sig_genes)
## [1] TRUE

Step 6: Y537S-specific genes

The paper splits the genes that change in mutant cells into two kinds (Figure 1C showed one example of each):

Category Changed in Y537S vs WT (no E2)? Responds to E2 in WT cells? Example
Ligand-independent yes yes CISH
Y537S-specific yes no KNL1

Ligand-independent genes are the normal estrogen genes, just switched on without estrogen. Y537S-specific genes are the new ones, and they are what Figure 1D is about. So we need to remove every gene that responds to E2 in WT cells.

Step 1 Read in the E2 vs DMSO (WT cells) results.

res_E2 <- read.csv("ERmut_DESeq2_WT_E2_vs_WT_veh.csv", header = T)

Step 2 Make a list of E2-regulated genes.

# genes that respond to E2 in WT cells (padj < 0.05, any fold change)
E2_genes_df <- subset(res_E2, padj < 0.05)
E2_genes <- E2_genes_df$ensembl_id

length(E2_genes)
## [1] 5735

Question: Here we used only padj < 0.05 and no fold-change cutoff. Why is it safer to be generous here? (Hint: we want to be sure a “Y537S-specific” gene really does not respond to E2. Being generous throws out any gene that responds to E2 even a little.)

Step 3 Remove the E2-regulated genes from our Up and Down lists.

# keep the up genes that are NOT in the E2 list
up_specific <- up_genes[!up_genes %in% E2_genes]

# keep the down genes that are NOT in the E2 list
down_specific <- down_genes[!down_genes %in% E2_genes]

length(up_specific)
## [1] 940
length(down_specific)
## [1] 1295

What is it doing?

  1. up_genes %in% E2_genes asks, for every up gene, “is this gene also in the E2 list?” (TRUE/FALSE).
  2. ! flips TRUE ↔︎ FALSE, so now the question is “is this gene NOT in the E2 list?”.
  3. up_genes[ ... ] keeps only the up genes where the answer was TRUE.

Step 4 Check our two example genes from Figure 1C. We look up their Ensembl IDs, then ask which list they are in.

example_ids <- res_YS |>
  dplyr::filter(symbol %in% c("CISH", "KNL1")) |>
  dplyr::select(symbol, ensembl_id)

example_ids$in_up_genes    <- example_ids$ensembl_id %in% up_genes
example_ids$in_E2_genes    <- example_ids$ensembl_id %in% E2_genes
example_ids$in_up_specific <- example_ids$ensembl_id %in% up_specific

example_ids
##   symbol      ensembl_id in_up_genes in_E2_genes in_up_specific
## 1   CISH ENSG00000114737        TRUE        TRUE          FALSE
## 2   KNL1 ENSG00000137812        TRUE       FALSE           TRUE

Question: Both genes are up in Y537S. Why is CISH removed but KNL1 kept?

Step 7: Function enrichGO()

From the clusterProfiler package, enrichGO() performs Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis to identify over-represented biological terms among a list of genes.

  1. There are ontology options: [“BP”, “MF”, “CC”]. The ont argument can accept either “BP” (Biological Process), “MF” (Molecular Function), and “CC” (Cellular Component) subontologies, or “ALL” for all three.

  2. There are keytypes options: this is the type of gene ID we give it. The options for org.Hs.eg.db are:

keytypes(org.Hs.eg.db)
##  [1] "ACCNUM"       "ALIAS"        "ENSEMBL"      "ENSEMBLPROT"  "ENSEMBLTRANS"
##  [6] "ENTREZID"     "ENZYME"       "EVIDENCE"     "EVIDENCEALL"  "GENENAME"    
## [11] "GENETYPE"     "GO"           "GOALL"        "IPI"          "MAP"         
## [16] "OMIM"         "ONTOLOGY"     "ONTOLOGYALL"  "PATH"         "PFAM"        
## [21] "PMID"         "PROSITE"      "REFSEQ"       "SYMBOL"       "UCSCKG"      
## [26] "UNIPROT"
  1. OrgDb: the annotation database for our organism. Our cells are human, so we use org.Hs.eg.db (for mouse it would be org.Mm.eg.db). The different organisms with annotation databases are listed here: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html#___Organism
#go_up <- enrichGO(gene = sig genes,
                  #universe = background genes,
                  #OrgDb = organism Db,
                  #keyType = 'type of gene ID',
                  #readable = T,
                  #ont = "BP",
                  #pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
                  #qvalueCutoff = 0.05)
Argument What to give it
gene Our significant genes: a vector of IDs (the marbles we grabbed)
universe The background genes: a vector of IDs (the whole bag). We use names(background_gene_list), because the IDs are the names of that vector
OrgDb The annotation database
keyType What kind of IDs are in gene and universe
readable = T Translate the gene IDs in the output to gene symbols, so we can read them
ont Which ontology to test
pvalueCutoff, qvalueCutoff Only report terms below these cutoffs

Together, we will run this next part. It will take about a minute to run.

Show solution 
go_up <- enrichGO(gene = up_specific,
                  universe = names(background_gene_list),
                  OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                  keyType = "ENSEMBL",
                  readable = T,
                  ont = "BP",
                  pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
                  qvalueCutoff = 0.05)

What is it doing?

It tests whether GO Biological Process (BP) terms are significantly enriched in our Y537S-specific Up genes (up_specific) compared to a background of all tested genes (background_gene_list), using human ENSEMBL gene IDs.

Tip: If something takes a long time to run, save it with saveRDS() so you can load it later with readRDS() instead of running it again.

go_up will be an object containing a table of significantly enriched GO terms, along with stats like:

  • p-value
  • q-value (adjusted p-value/FDR)
  • number of genes in each term
  • gene symbols

Column Meaning
ID, Description The GO term accession number and name
GeneRatio (our genes in this term) / (our genes that have any GO annotation)
BgRatio (background genes in this term) / (background genes that have any GO annotation)
FoldEnrichment GeneRatio ÷ BgRatio: how many times more of our genes are in this term than expected by chance
pvalue, p.adjust, qvalue The p-value from the hypergeometric test, and two ways of correcting it for testing thousands of terms
geneID The symbols of our genes in this term, separated by /
Count How many of our genes are in this term

Question: Read the top 10 Descriptions. What do they have in common? Do they match “Mitosis” at the top of Figure 1D? Is KNL1 in any of them? (Search cluster_summary_up$geneID.)

Visualizing clusterProfiler results

clusterProfiler has a variety of options for viewing the over-represented GO terms.

The bar plot is the most widely used method to visualize enriched terms. It depicts the enrichment scores (e.g. p values) and gene count or ratio as bar height and color. Users can specify the number of terms (most significant) or selected terms to display via the showCategory parameter.

bar_up <- barplot(go_up,
                  showCategory = 10,
                  title = "Y537S-specific Up: GO Biological Process",
                  font.size = 8)

bar_up

The dot plot adds one more piece of information: the x-axis is the GeneRatio, the dot size is the number of genes (Count), and the color is the adjusted p-value.

dot_up <- dotplot(go_up,
                  showCategory = 10,
                  title = "Y537S-specific Up",
                  font.size = 8)
dot_up

Question: Why do so many of the top terms sound alike (“chromosome segregation”, “nuclear division”, “organelle fission”)? (Hint: one gene can belong to many GO terms, and GO terms are nested: “nuclear division” is a part of “organelle fission”.)

“Black Trail” Exercise 2: the Down genes

Scenario: Jordan, a graduate student in the lab, has a hypothesis: mutant ER doesn’t just turn on cell-division genes, it also turns down genes that help the immune system recognize the tumor. If that’s true, immune-related terms should come up for the Y537S-specific Down genes.

Help Jordan run enrichGO() on the Down genes, save the result as go_down, and make a dot plot called dot_down with the top 10 terms.

Hint: Copy your enrichGO() code from Exercise 7.1. Only one argument needs to change.

Show solution 
go_down <- enrichGO(gene = down_specific,
                    universe = names(background_gene_list),
                    OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                    keyType = "ENSEMBL",
                    readable = T,
                    ont = "BP",
                    pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
                    qvalueCutoff = 0.05)

cluster_summary_down <- data.frame(go_down)

#write.csv(cluster_summary_down, "GO_BP_Y537S_specific_down.csv")

head(cluster_summary_down$Description, 10)
##  [1] "negative regulation of viral genome replication"                                                                  
##  [2] "negative regulation of viral process"                                                                             
##  [3] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway, TAP-independent"
##  [4] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class Ib"                               
##  [5] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway"                 
##  [6] "antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class Ib"                                          
##  [7] "regulation of viral life cycle"                                                                                   
##  [8] "positive regulation of T cell mediated cytotoxicity"                                                              
##  [9] "antigen processing and presentation via MHC class Ib"                                                             
## [10] "regulation of viral process"
dot_down <- dotplot(go_down,
                    showCategory = 10,
                    title = "Y537S-specific Down",
                    font.size = 8)
dot_down

Was Jordan right? Look for terms about the immune / interferon response or antigen presentation.

Up vs Down in one plot: compareCluster()

Figure 1D shows up and down terms together. So far we ran enrichGO() twice, once for each list. compareCluster() runs enrichGO() on several gene lists at once and puts the results side by side in one plot.

# BASIC USAGE
## DO NOT RUN
#compareCluster(geneClusters = list(Name1 = genes1, Name2 = genes2),
               #fun = "enrichGO",
               #...the same arguments we gave enrichGO...)
Argument What to give it
geneClusters A named list of gene vectors. The names (Up, Down) become the column labels in the plot
fun Which enrichment function to run on each list. Here "enrichGO"
everything else The same arguments we gave enrichGO(): universe, OrgDb, keyType, ont, readable. Notice there is no gene = argument; the genes come from geneClusters 
go_compare <- compareCluster(geneClusters = list(Up = up_specific,
                                                 Down = down_specific),
                             fun = "enrichGO",
                             universe = names(background_gene_list),
                             OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                             keyType = "ENSEMBL",
                             ont = "BP",
                             readable = T)

What is it doing?

It runs enrichGO() once on up_specific and once on down_specific, with the same background, and keeps both results together in one object called go_compare. It takes about as long as running enrichGO() twice.

go_compare_plot <- dotplot(go_compare,
                           showCategory = 8,
                           title = "GO terms: Y537S-specific genes",
                           font.size = 9,
                           label_format = 50)
go_compare_plot

  • showCategory = 8 shows the top 8 terms from each list.
  • The x-axis now shows the two lists (Up and Down); the numbers under the labels are how many genes in each list have a GO annotation.
  • Some GO term names are very long. label_format = 50 wraps the y-axis labels after 50 characters so they don’t overlap.

Question: What does it mean biologically that mutant ER turns up cell-division genes and turns down immune-response genes? (Think about the cells growing faster and the tumor hiding from the immune system.)

Save the figure.

ggsave("Fig1D_GO_dotplot_Y537S.png", go_compare_plot, width = 9, height = 8)

A Figure 1D-style table

Figure 1D is actually a table, not a plot: the GO term, the direction (↑ or ↓), and the p-value. Let’s build one from our results with the top 5 terms in each direction.

Step 1 Take the top 5 Up terms and add a Direction column.

top_up <- cluster_summary_up |>
  dplyr::arrange(p.adjust) |>          # smallest adjusted p-value first
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |>          # keep the first 5 rows
  dplyr::mutate(Direction = "↑")       # add a column that says "up"

top_up$Description
## [1] "chromosome segregation"                   
## [2] "nuclear division"                         
## [3] "nuclear chromosome segregation"           
## [4] "organelle fission"                        
## [5] "positive regulation of cell cycle process"
  • arrange(p.adjust) sorts the rows from the most to the least significant term.
  • slice_head(n = 5) keeps the first 5 rows.
  • mutate() adds a new column, Direction, with the same value (↑) in every row.

Step 2 Do the same for the Down terms.

top_down <- cluster_summary_down |>
  dplyr::arrange(p.adjust) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Direction = "↓")

top_down$Description
## [1] "negative regulation of viral genome replication"                                                                  
## [2] "negative regulation of viral process"                                                                             
## [3] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway, TAP-independent"
## [4] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class Ib"                               
## [5] "antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway"

Step 3 Stack the two tables, sort by p-value, and keep only the three columns in the paper.

fig1d_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(top_up, top_down) |>                        # 1. stack the rows
  dplyr::arrange(p.adjust) |>                                               # 2. sort by p-value
  dplyr::mutate(P = formatC(p.adjust, format = "e", digits = 1)) |>          # 3. write P like the paper
  dplyr::select(`Gene ontology (Y537S genes)` = Description, Direction, P)  # 4. pick and rename columns

knitr::kable(fig1d_table, row.names = FALSE)
Gene ontology (Y537S genes) Direction P
chromosome segregation ↑ 4.6e-14
nuclear division ↑ 1.7e-13
nuclear chromosome segregation ↑ 3.3e-12
organelle fission ↑ 2.0e-11
positive regulation of cell cycle process ↑ 2.0e-11
negative regulation of viral genome replication ↓ 5.2e-06
negative regulation of viral process ↓ 1.4e-05
antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway, TAP-independent ↓ 2.6e-05
antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class Ib ↓ 3.2e-05
antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen via MHC class I via ER pathway ↓ 3.2e-05

What is each line doing?

  1. bind_rows() puts top_down underneath top_up: 5 + 5 = 10 rows. This works because both tables have the same columns.
  2. arrange(p.adjust) sorts all 10 terms together, so the most significant term is at the top no matter which direction it came from (like the paper).
  3. formatC(..., format = "e", digits = 1) writes small numbers in scientific notation with one decimal, e.g. 0.0000000000000231 becomes 2.3e-14. The paper writes it as 2.3E-14.
  4. select() keeps only 3 columns. Writing new name = old name inside select() renames a column at the same time. The backticks (`) let us use a column name with spaces and brackets.
  5. knitr::kable() prints the data frame as a nice-looking table when you knit.

Question: Put your table next to the orange Y537S table in Figure 1D. Which of your terms are the same as, or similar to, the paper’s?

Save the table.

write.csv(fig1d_table, "Fig1D_GO_table_Y537S.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Compare with Figure 1D

  1. Is “Mitosis” (or something like it) at the top of your Up list, like in the paper?
  2. The paper lists terms like “Vacuole” and “Chromatin binding”. We only tested ont = "BP". What would you change to get terms like these?
  3. The paper’s p-values (e.g. 9.1E-101) are much smaller than ours. The paper used a different tool (Illumina BaseSpace Correlation Engine), unadjusted p-values, and two mutants (Y537S and D538G) to define their gene lists. List two reasons why our numbers could differ.
  4. Many of our top Up terms are near-duplicates (“nuclear division”, “organelle fission”). The paper shows just “Mitosis”. If you have time, look up clusterProfiler::simplify(), which merges redundant terms.

Key columns we used today:

File / object Column Used for
ERmut_normalized_counts.csv symbol finding CISH, KNL1 and GREB1
sample columns bar plots
sample_annotations.csv group, ER_status relative expression, bar order, bar color
ERmut_DESeq2_YS_veh_vs_WT_veh.csv ensembl_id gene IDs for enrichGO()
log2FoldChange, padj significant in Y537S? up or down?
ERmut_DESeq2_WT_E2_vs_WT_veh.csv padj E2-regulated in WT? (to remove)
go_up / go_down Description GO term names
GeneRatio, Count dot plot x-axis and dot size
p.adjust color, ranking, and P in the table
